Session timeouts#

Open sesame opens the door for a live session; a stale one finds it locked. This page is about the two clocks every signed-in session runs on and the settings that control them. When you have tuned them, see Requiring MFA, which ages the sign-in time the same clocks record.

The two clocks#

Every signed-in session has two clocks. The idle timeout is the quiet time after which the session is dropped, and the absolute lifetime is the longest a session may live, no matter how active it is. Both are in minutes, and both are checked on every user() call, so a stale session is signed out on the spot the first time anything asks who is signed in.

Key Default Meaning
session.idle_minutes 120 Drop the session after this much quiet time.
session.absolute_minutes 720 End the session this long after sign-in, even if it is still active.
logoutReuseTtlSeconds 60 The window in which a reused logged-out session ID is logged as an anomaly, in seconds. A new NativeSession() option, not a config key; 0 makes invalidate() destroy the session outright instead of leaving the logout marker.
checkSessionSettings null How a native session treats session.use_strict_mode, session.use_only_cookies and the session cookie's flags. A new NativeSession() option, not a config key. null turns both settings on whenever no session is active and warns once per request (E_USER_WARNING) when the app started its session with either one off, or with a cookie that lacks HttpOnly, Secure (on https) or a Lax or Strict SameSite; true also turns the settings on but throws LogicException on every call instead of warning; false leaves the settings alone and stays quiet. SESAME never sets a cookie flag.

How the clocks are checked#

On login the session stores the sign-in time and the last activity time, and user() refreshes the last activity time on every call that finds a live session. A session made before the timeouts existed (a user, no timestamps) counts as expired.

Regeneration grace#

On login the session ID is regenerated. For the native PHP session the old ID is not deleted at once: it is marked with a "destroyed at" time and the new ID and kept for a 60 second grace, so a user whose browser is still sending the old ID after a slow network does not lose the login. After the grace, any use of the old ID is treated as a possible hijack: the session is retired, a clean one is started, and sesame.session_anomaly is logged as a warning with reason destroyed_session_reused. Pass graceSeconds: 0 to new NativeSession() to restore the old behavior, where the old session is deleted at once. Laravel uses the framework's own regenerate.

Logout reuse window#

When invalidate() retires a session it leaves a "logged out at" marker in the session store itself, under the same ID. The marker lives in the store, not in process memory, so no extra cache is needed and every worker sees the same marker. A later request that presents that ID is not revived: the marked session is retired, a fresh empty one starts, and while the reuse window lasts (60 seconds by default, the logoutReuseTtlSeconds option of new NativeSession()) the reuse is logged once with reason logged_out_session_reused. Past the window the marked session is still retired, just not logged. Pass logoutReuseTtlSeconds: 0 to turn the check off: the session is destroyed outright on logout, the old behavior.

In Laravel#

In Laravel the keys are SESAME_SESSION_IDLE_MINUTES and SESAME_SESSION_ABSOLUTE_MINUTES.
